segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat bread.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “And why do you yourselves break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For God said, ‘Honor your father and mother,’ and, ‘Whoever speaks ill of father or mother must be put to death.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But you say, ‘Whoever says to his father or mother, “Whatever help you might have had from me is an offering,”

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: is not to honor his father.’ So you have nullified the word of God for the sake of your tradition.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Hypocrites! Isaiah prophesied well about you when he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far away from me;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: they worship me in vain, teaching human commands as doctrines.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And calling the crowd to him, he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Listen and understand:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth, this defiles a person.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the disciples came and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do you know that the Pharisees took offense when they heard this saying?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Every plant that my heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Leave them; they are blind guides of the blind. And if a blind person guides a blind person, both will fall into a pit.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Explain this parable to us.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Are even you still without understanding?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Do you not see that everything that goes into the mouth passes into the stomach and is expelled into the latrine?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But the things that come out of the mouth come from the heart, and those defile a person.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, acts of sexual immorality, thefts, false testimonies, slanders.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: These are the things that defile a person; but eating with unwashed hands does not defile a person.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And leaving there, Jesus withdrew to the region of Tyre and Sidon.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And look, a Canaanite woman from that territory came out and kept crying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David! My daughter is severely tormented by a demon.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he did not answer her a word. And his disciples came and kept asking him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Send her away, because she keeps crying out after us.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But she came and bowed down before him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, help me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the little dogs.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Yes, Lord, for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus answered her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you wish.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And her daughter was healed from that hour.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Moving on from there, Jesus went along beside the Sea of Galilee, and he went up the mountain and sat down there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Large crowds came to him, bringing with them people who were mute, blind, lame, crippled, and many others, and they set them down at his feet, and he healed them,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that the crowd was amazed when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled made sound, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. And they glorified the God of Israel.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus called his disciples to him and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “I have compassion on the crowd, because they have stayed with me three days now and have nothing to eat. I do not want to send them away hungry, or they may collapse on the way.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The disciples said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Where in a deserted place could we get so many loaves as to satisfy so large a crowd?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “How many loaves do you have?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Seven, and a few small fish.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And directing the crowd to recline on the ground,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he took the seven loaves and the fish, and after giving thanks he broke them and kept giving them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They all ate and were satisfied, and they picked up what was left over of the broken pieces, seven baskets full.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And after sending the crowds away, he got into the boat and went to the territory of Magadan.

notes.note: This refers to a body of rulings handed down by earlier teachers and treated by the Pharisees as binding alongside the written Law. The handwashing at issue was a matter of ritual purity, not hygiene; the Law of Moses does not require it of ordinary people before meals. “Eat bread” is a Semitic way of saying “have a meal.”

The Greek word is the ordinary Septuagint term for something offered to God; Mark’s parallel gives the Hebrew word, korban. A person could vow that property was dedicated in this way, which put it out of other people’s reach. Jesus’ charge is that the tradition let such a vow override the duty to support one’s parents.

notes.phrase: is not to honor his father
notes.note: The Greek is an emphatic negative, literally “will certainly not honor,” in a sentence that is grammatically broken off. Most translations soften it to “need not honor,” a release from obligation. It can equally be read as the wording of the ruling itself, which holds the son to his vow and so forbids him to help; the rendering here keeps that stronger sense. “Honor” in this context includes material support.
Manuscripts vary here between “the word,” “the law” and “the commandment” of God; the sense is little affected. Many manuscripts also add “or his mother” after “his father.”

The Greek verb literally means “to make common.” In Jewish Greek it had become a technical term for making someone or something ritually unclean, unfit for contact with what is holy. The dispute is about purity before God, not about dirt or health.

notes.traditional: a woman of Canaan / a Canaanite woman
notes.note: “Canaanite” was an archaic term by the first century; Mark’s parallel calls her a Greek, Syrophoenician by birth. Matthew’s word recalls the ancient inhabitants of the land in Israel’s Scriptures and marks her plainly as a Gentile outsider, which sharpens the exchange that follows.

The verb describes the physical act of bowing or prostrating oneself before a superior, whether a god, a king, or someone whose help is being begged. Older versions have “worshiped”; most modern versions have “knelt.” Here it is the gesture of a desperate petitioner, and the text does not say how much more she meant by it.

The Greek uses a diminutive form, not the ordinary word for dog. Diminutives had often lost their force in the Greek of this period, so “dogs” is a possible rendering; but the picture of animals under the family table suggests household dogs, not street scavengers. Whether the diminutive softens the saying is debated; “dogs” was in any case a term Jews could use for Gentiles.

Most translations have “Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs,” as though she were objecting. The Greek connective means “for indeed” or “for even,” not “but.” She accepts his image and argues from within it: the dogs get fed too, without the children losing their bread. The word for “masters” is the plural of the word she uses to address Jesus as “Lord.”

This is a different Greek word from the “baskets” of the feeding of the five thousand (14:20). It denotes a larger hamper, the kind in which Paul was lowered from the wall of Damascus (Acts 9:25). Matthew keeps the two words distinct when Jesus recalls both feedings in 16:9–10.

The earliest manuscripts read Magadan, a place otherwise unknown. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read Magdala, a known town on the western shore of the lake. Mark’s parallel has Dalmanutha, which is equally obscure.

candidates.reason: It recurs across the Gospels and Revelation, where the choice between “worship,” “kneel” and “bow down” carries Christological weight and should not vary without reason.
It is frequent across the Gospels and Paul, and translators vary between “offend,” “cause to stumble” and “fall away,” so the senses need to be fixed once.
It appears in vice lists and the divorce sayings throughout the New Testament, and “fornication,” “sexual immorality” and “prostitution” give readers quite different impressions.
It is very frequent in the Gospels, and “scribe” suggests a copyist to modern readers where the word means a trained legal scholar.
It recurs throughout the Synoptics, and the traditional “demon-possessed” imports an idea of ownership the Greek verb does not state.
